column3: Exact parallel: divine signs recited in truth make the question of any later discourse a challenge to belief after the signs.
The call to reverent restraint supplies only a broad ethical backdrop to refusal of the concluding question.
It keeps the temporal term open to a restorative reading: belief may follow wrongdoing through repentance, rather than only be refused after a warning.
It presents belief in the Lord's signs as the positive response whose absence 77:50 questions.
It begins the immediate sequence that makes 77:50 a verdict after the deniers are directed toward what they denied.
Exact parallel after an appeal to observe creation and mortality; it frames another discourse as an evasion of evidence already displayed.
Its repeated question about denying favors parallels the interrogative pressure, though its object is favors rather than later discourse.
The repeated woe identifies the deniers whose settled response leads into the final question.
It distinguishes divergent responses to the same matter: some believe and some turn away, without making a later discourse decisive.
A second favor-refrain reinforces the rhetorical demand for response, with a different stated object.
Its woe refrain immediately precedes the final refusal scene and preserves the local accusatory cadence.
It depicts nonbelief as an already operative refusal, a possible background for why further speech will not be believed.
The recurring favor-refrain offers a parallel challenge to denial without equating favors and hadith.
It contrasts the rescue of believers with the local fate of deniers, but adds no discourse language.
It supplies a positive outcome for believers, counterbalancing 77:50's focus on those who will not believe.
A direct question about why they do not believe closely parallels 77:50 while leaving its wider cosmic setting distinct.
It continues the ordered movement of the deniers through the judgment scene that culminates in 77:50.
It links professed belief with fidelity to entrusted obligations, a secondary account of what belief entails.
It shows hadith as a delivered account of Moses that can make a past event present; this broadens, rather than replaces, 77:50's rhetorical use of hadith.
Their refusal when told to bow is the nearest enacted example of the nonbelief asked about in 77:50.
A newly arriving reminder is heard playfully, offering a contrary reception of renewed speech rather than a direct parallel.
It again uses hadith to introduce Moses' account, preserving the narrative sense of the term as a secondary reading.
The final woe immediately before 77:50 marks the deniers addressed by its question.
It makes a hadith announce an encompassing event, supporting a report-event sense alongside the challenge in 77:50.
It distinguishes engagement with the signs from another hadith, showing that discourse can be a social setting requiring separation.
The watched judgment and command to endure offer contextual evidence imagery but no close link to 77:50.
A past military account functions as present evidence; this is a narrative analogue for hadith, not an answer to the question.
It pairs belief in signs with mercy and post-wrongdoing repentance, a secondary positive response after failure.
It negates the apparent shade as protection, sharpening the judgment setting behind the final question.
The earth's reporting makes events themselves evidentiary, preserving an alternative to merely verbal testimony.
Its trust after divine aid is a distant belief-related use of the temporal language.
The protected setting of the reverent contrasts with the deniers' ineffective shade in the same passage.
It uses afterness for an unforeseen matter that may arise, preserving temporal openness rather than a fixed later speech.
Its afterness concerns the absence of a descending force after a person, with little bearing on belief in discourse.
Brief enjoyment for offenders supplies the local contrast before the repeated woe and 77:50.
It calls the message hadith and shows the messenger's grief at refusal, while limiting any claim that persuasion can be forced.
It treats hadith as lingering social conversation and afterness in a separate legal instruction.
Brief enjoyment followed by compulsion to punishment parallels the nearby sequence's warning structure.
A pressured profession of belief may contrast provisional crisis-response with lasting belief, but remains indirect.
It directly challenges a dismissive or compromising reception of this hadith, a close contrary response to 77:50's demand for belief.
The immense sparks continue the visual evidence and threat to which the deniers in 77:50 have been exposed.
It rejects reducing the message to poetic speech while noting scant belief, directly clarifying a rival classification of discourse.
It challenges astonishment at this hadith; together with its call not to be heedless, it parallels refusal to receive the warning.
Desired fruits form the positive counterpart to the preceding punitive scene and distinguish the two responses' outcomes.
It states belief, the Last Day, and righteous action with release from fear and grief, a positive but broader counterpart.
Earlier recipients believe in it, preserving continuity rather than treating a new message as disqualifying.
The command to eat and drink in return for deeds completes the local contrast with the deniers' doom.
Later settlement after oppressors offers only a distant temporal pattern of reversal.
It raises whether those who denied before destruction would believe, a judgment-pattern parallel to 77:50's question.
A secure station for the reverent contrasts with the insecure fate developed in 77, without discourse language.
Belief followed by increased guidance supplies a positive developmental trajectory, unlike the refusal in 77:50.
The demand to bring forebears is a specific evidentiary challenge, only broadly related to disbelief.
The camel-like yellow sparks extend the immediate warning whose rejection is named in the final question.
Witnessed persecution of believers shows belief persisting under public pressure, a secondary contrast to the deniers.
Calling the message fabricated is presented as bound to nonbelief, directly identifying a hostile alternative reading of the discourse.
Gardens and springs extend the secure-state contrast with 77's judgment scenes.
Provision and safety provide a distinct register of divine favor; they can illuminate belief's security associations without defining 77:50.
It shows reversal to ingratitude after a visible adverse sign, a temporal pattern of refusal after evidence.
The repeated woe continues the cadence that leads to the final challenge.
Repentance after punishment preserves a possible later turning, qualifying a purely closed temporal inference.
Being turned away from it supplies a contrary account of why the discourse fails to reach some hearers.
It identifies the message as a descent from the Lord of the worlds, directly supporting the source side of the discourse question.
The demand for a discourse like it is a rhetorical test of the claim, though the associated auxiliary reading remains speculative.
Hadith introduces Abraham's honored guests, another narrative use that keeps report and event together.
The day when they do not speak follows the warning sequence and confirms the finality of their rejected response.
The statement that punishment is not secure has only a remote root-level association with belief and security.
It explicitly denies that the narratives are fabricated hadith and presents them as confirmation, explanation, guidance, and mercy for believers.
Calling the message a reminder for all worlds offers a concise positive designation alongside 77:50's question about further speech.
Its after-truth question frames departure from established truth as misguidance, closely analogous in structure but with a different noun.
It requires leaving assemblies that mock the signs until another hadith begins, distinguishing discourse contexts rather than endorsing a preferred reading.
Their lack of permission to make excuses is the local consequence of the denial that 77:50 exposes.
It attributes failed response to the absence of belief and also preserves a contested account of responsibility among deceivers and followers.
The brothers imagine becoming righteous after wrongdoing, a distant and morally contrary use of afterness.
The repeated woe anchors the deniers' culpability immediately before the separation-day declaration.
Signs in heavens and earth are for believers, providing the evidentiary setting that the exact parallel in 45:6 then invokes.
Repeated messengers and repeated denial turn communities into accounts, joining hadith, rejection, and exemplary history.
It distinguishes those who already believe from those who will not, a limited background for persistent refusal.
The community's misguidance after Moses concerns succession and testing, only distantly related to later discourse.
Taking the calf after Moses is an instance of post-sign betrayal but adds no close speech or belief relation.
The day of separation gathers all generations, giving the adjudicative setting for the passage's repeated condemnation.
It warns that belief can be internally compromised by association, a qualifying reading of what it means to believe.
Earlier rejection shapes reception of later clear proofs, closely supporting the persistence of refusal implied by 77:50.
The ark is made under watch and revelation; this gives auxiliary source-and-guidance imagery, not a replacement sense for hadith.
Life after death is a broad sign of reversal, with only a distant temporal connection.
The calf after Moses repeats a post-sign betrayal pattern but remains remote from the discourse question.
The challenge to produce a scheme in the judgment scene is a local counterpart to the passage's exposure of powerless denial.
Publicly declared belief calls for hearing and response, offering a positive interpersonal contrast.
Later dwelling in the land and final gathering concern historical sequence, not reception of discourse.
Diversionary hadith is purchased to lead away from the way, preserving a direct contrary category of speech alongside the implied true discourse.
A sign is stated to be for believers, supporting evidence-responsive belief in a different narrative setting.
The favor-refrain repeats the interrogative accusation of denial while retaining its distinct object.
Believers receive a reminder after a warning of punishment, a broad but indirect reminder-belief link.
Nonbelief follows an established pattern among earlier peoples, supporting a historical account of repeated refusal.
It concerns honor and hypocrisy within a community; its belief reference is not closely tied to 77:50.
Nonbelief in divine signs is paired with withheld guidance and painful punishment, matching the warning logic broadly.
It contrasts guidance and division through a formula of belief, but has no specific discourse or afterness connection.
Doubt and hesitation characterize those who do not believe, offering a psychological contrast to assent.
Belief joined with righteous deeds yields an unfailing reward, a general positive counterpart only.
Believers are persecuted precisely for belief, showing an external contrary response to faithful assent.
Belief conditions acknowledged striving toward the hereafter, a general outcome-focused contrast.
On the judgment day, no discourse can be concealed from God; this gives a secondary disclosure-and-accountability setting for hadith.
The charge that they scarcely comprehend hadith supplies a reception-based account of failure before divine discourse.
The question of who is truer than God in hadith directly grounds 77:50's challenge in the trustworthiness of divine speech.
The call to produce a surah like it if in doubt provides a parallel test of the message's unmatched standing.
The fabrication claim is answered by a challenge to bring a comparable surah, preserving a contrary accusation and its test.
The challenge to bring ten fabricated surahs extends the same rival claim without resolving it by preference.
God's sending of the best hadith gives a direct positive designation for the discourse whose replacement 77:50 questions.
The instruction not to listen to the Quran and to drown it out identifies an active contrary response to the message.
The incapacity of humans and jinn to produce the like of the Quran provides a broader analogue to the challenge of a later discourse.
Their turning away from the reminder parallels the refusal of the already delivered warning that 77:50 presses.
Their refusal to prostrate when the Quran is recited gives an enacted reception-failure alongside the question of belief.
Those who deny this hadith are explicitly named and warned, making it a close parallel to the deniers in 77:50.
